reverse_outline.summary: Three-point preview: checkout commits the order once, later facts arrive as unreliable messages handled with keys and separate states, and the order ends as single-issuer documents reconciled monthly
Opening failure: a paid order still shows as unpaid, leaving warehouse and support stuck
The company lacks a shared order record; each chapter opens on one of its failures
After payment, provider, warehouse and carrier report via messages that can be late, out of order or duplicated
The part's rules, one per system: single order creation, keyed messages with one writer per money movement, separate order states, ledger matched to bank
Running example timeline: Eva's €235 order from creation through payment confirmation, invoice and bank match
Checkout chapter preview: creating exactly one order despite retries, not depending on the thank-you page
Payments chapter preview: payment lifecycle, with duplicate refunds showing the need for one writer and a retry identifier
Order management chapter preview: one order home with separate states, handling partial completion, and when to adopt an OMS
Tax and ledger chapter preview: linking orders, invoices, payouts and bank, with single-issuer invoice numbering, VAT split and Peppol delivery tracking
Callback resolving the unpaid order (provider message marks it paid) and pointer to start with checkout

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.quote: Eva's €235 splits into €194.21 net and €40.79 value-added tax.
results.finding: The tax-split numbers are stated with no sentence saying what they show; the spec's 'shows' (the invoice carries the tax split, the order ends as documents) is not given, so the figures read as a bare fact between the invoice-sequence and Peppol sentences.

results.quote: Once the click on "pay" turns the catalog's facts into an order, a **payment service provider (PSP)** reports the money through a **webhook**
results.finding: Declared cause_effect carrying over the failures, starting with the paid order that reads unpaid: the paragraph gives the mechanism but never ties it back to the opening ('this is why the order reads unpaid'); flowB: 'it never says outright that the missing webhook is why the order looks unpaid; that link waits until the last section'. The previous-page hand-off ('the catalog's facts') is also not anchored (both flow readers).

results.quote: **Where we are in the order's journey.** Eva's order, the book's running example, goes right.
results.finding: Declared contrast with the failures of the months before April 2027 and the four rules: 'goes right' implies a contrast but the failures are not picked up and no contrast marker is used; both flow readers had to infer it (flowA: 'the text never says so'; flowB: 'a contrast word would help').

results.quote: finance matches the payout with the bank at April's close in May.
results.finding: Declared elaboration as a sentence at the end of the previous unit, carrying over the four rules and the company whose failures open the chapters: Eva's paragraph ends on the May close with no sentence leading into the chapter list; only the heading marks the turn.

results.quote: The company has no shared order record yet, and each chapter opens on another of its failures before April 2027.
results.finding: Both flow readers mark this paragraph's position unclear: it breaks the step from the opening scene to its explanation, talks about the chapters in the middle of the setup, and 'before April 2027' has no anchor until Eva's paragraph. The difficulty comes from the declared order (p05 was moved here after round 3; the round-3 readers objected to the opposite position), so the spec has to settle where p05 goes, or whether its chapter clause belongs in the chapter list.
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3 ('The company has no shared order record yet… I re-read this. "Before April 2027" has no anchor'); also flowB item 2 marks it 'partly unclear'

results.quote: Once the click on "pay" turns the catalog's facts into an order
results.finding: 'The catalog's facts' leans on Part II without saying so; flowA: 'Which "catalog's facts"? … I had to infer it.'
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3 ('"The catalog's facts" seems to point back to an earlier part and is not explained')

results.quote: The ledger is written from invoices and payout reports, which list the provider's transfers to the merchant, and matched with the bank monthly.
results.finding: The relative clause splits 'written from…' from 'and matched with…'; flowA: 'I re-read this.'
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3 ('Dense; the relative clause separates "written" from "and matched"; read twice')

results.quote: The provider confirms it seconds later.
results.finding: The success case is not said to contrast with the opening failure; flowA: 'The opposite of the opening scene, but the text never says so; I had to work out that the opening failure was a different order.'
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3 ('"Eva's order… goes right." Clear only on reflection that it contrasts with the opening failure; a contrast word would help')

results.quote: finance matches the payout with the bank at April's close in May.
results.finding: 'April's close in May' made both readers pause; flowA: 'Re-read to separate April's close from May.'
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3 ('"at April's close in May" made me pause')

results.quote: A Belgian wholesale invoice sent through Peppol, the network for structured invoices, shows why its issuer must also record its delivery or rejection.
results.finding: Wholesale and invoice delivery/rejection arrive new in the last line; flowA: 'slightly out of place'.
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3 ('The Peppol sentence brings in delivery or rejection in the last line; followable but the densest spot')

results.quote: Together, the chapters explain the opening's unpaid order
results.finding: Both readers find 'Together' overstated: the answer comes mainly from the first two chapters; flowA: '"Together" overstates a little.'
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3 ('The answer comes mainly from the first two chapters; the opening's warehouse and support problems are never picked up again')

results.quote: It asks every owner for a final answer and creates the order exactly once, while owning none of the facts it writes.
results.finding: flowA: 'Hard on first contact; nothing before the chapter list explains it.'

results.quote: So the part sets rules, one chapter for each of four systems that handle the order in turn.
results.finding: flowA: the rules do not map one-to-one onto the systems and the four systems are never listed in the sentence; 'I worked them out from Figure 1.'

results.quote: At the payment provider, every message carries a key, so a repeat changes nothing, and each money movement has one writer.
results.finding: flowB: KEY POINT 2 says every message carries a key, warehouse and carrier included; here the key is placed only at the payment provider. 'Small mismatch.'

results.quote: One writer per money movement, one invoice sequence per legal entity, and a monthly match of orders, payouts and the bank.
results.finding: flowA: KEY POINTS bullet 3 puts 'One writer per money movement' under documents and the ledger, while the body gives that rule to payments. 'Small mismatch.' (The callout is the author's wording.)

results.quote: an identifier shared across retries
results.finding: flowA: terminology shift from 'every message carries a key' to 'an identifier shared across retries'; 'I paused to check whether these are the same thing.'

results.quote: the ledger is fed by documents, not events
results.finding: flowB: 'a contrast the body never sets up.' flowA separately found the two back-to-back figures partly overlapping ('Why two figures back to back that partly overlap is unclear'); flowB found them 'a little heavy, but not confusing', so not the same point.

results.quote: Eva's payment redirect to her bank's app shows why order creation cannot depend on the thank-you page.
results.finding: flowB: the thank-you page first appears here; 'the opening scene never mentioned it, so the close's answer rests on a thread that only appears here.' (The decision log declined adding it to the opening for length.)

results.quote: Invoices are numbered in one unbroken sequence per legal entity, a company billing in its own name, so only one system may issue them.
results.finding: flowB: 'The gloss in the middle gets in the way of the cause-and-effect; re-read.'

results.quote: So the order keeps separate states for money, parcels and returns, and every message carries a key.
results.finding: Terms reader: 'key' is used in KEY POINTS before the rules paragraph says what it does, is never tied to Part I's idempotency, and the later 'identifier shared across retries' is never said to be the same key.
results.corroborated_by: flowA item 3 ('Terminology shift: "every message carries a key" vs "an identifier shared across retries". I paused to check whether these are the same thing.')

results.quote: One writer per money movement, one invoice sequence per legal entity, and a monthly match of orders, payouts and the bank.
results.finding: Terms reader: 'invoice sequence per legal entity' and 'payouts' are used in KEY POINTS before they are explained (payout in ¶4, legal entity and the unbroken sequence only in Chapters ¶4). No flow reader reported them unexplained; payout is glossed in the draft as the spec asks.

results.quote: The ledger is written from invoices and payout reports, which list the provider's transfers to the merchant, and matched with the bank monthly.
results.finding: Terms reader: 'the ledger' (also a station in Figures 1 and 2) is never said to be finance's book of accounts and is not in already_knows. No flow reader reported it.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶4 (Figure 1 caption); Chapters in this part ¶2
results.quote: the payment provider settles it
results.finding: Terms reader: 'settlement' and 'collection' are not glossed and 'settles' in Figure 1's caption cannot be followed yet. Both are on does_not_know and the draft never gives them; the spec says they are 'only named here' and its own Figure 1 evidence uses 'settles', so the draft follows the spec.
results.corroborated_by: does_not_know[0] ('Authorization, collection and settlement as stages of a payment … only named here'); the draft never gives them

results.quote: finance matches the payout with the bank at April's close in May.
results.finding: Terms reader: month-end close is accounting jargon not in already_knows; '"April's close in May" reads like a contradiction.'
results.corroborated_by: flowA item 3 ('Re-read to separate April's close from May') and flowB item 3 ('"at April's close in May" made me pause')
